# BRIEF IN SUPPORT OF DEFENDANT'S MOTION TO DISMISS

## ARGUMENT

The doctrine of qualified immunity shields officials from liability. See
Harlow v. Fitzgerald, 457 U.S. 800, 818 (1982). The Supreme Court reaffirmed
this standard in Pearson v. Callahan, 555 U.S. 223 (2009), and courts apply
it routinely. Id. at 236.

A plaintiff must plead facts sufficient to state a plausible claim. Bell
Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 570 (2007); Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556
U.S. 662 (2009). As the Court explained in Twombly, 550 U.S. at 555, labels
and conclusions will not suffice.

The Tenth Circuit has applied this framework. Aves v. Shah, 997 F.2d 762, 767
(10th Cir. 1993). Accord Bogus v. Nobody, 33 Umbrella 422, 425 (2020).

Federal courts retain discretion in these matters. See Tinch v. Video Indus.
Servs., Inc., 2019 WL 1396975 (E.D. Mich. Mar. 27, 2019). See also 42 U.S.C.
§ 1983.

The rule stated in Smith v. Fictional Reporter Co., 88 Jurisprudentia 100
(9th Cir. 2018), is not to the contrary.
